prompt: How many fewer hydrogens does benzene (C6H6) have than cyclohexane (C6H12)?
explanation: Benzene, C6H6, has six fewer hydrogens than the six-carbon cycloalkane cyclohexane, C6H12, so it is clearly unsaturated. It is usually drawn as a six-membered ring with alternating double and single bonds.

prompt: How does benzene's reaction with Br2 differ from cyclohexene's?

choices.text: Benzene reacts slowly by substitution, giving C6H5Br; cyclohexene reacts rapidly by addition
Both react rapidly by addition, giving dibromides
choices.why: Benzene fails to undergo typical alkene additions; it gives the substitution product C6H5Br.

choices.text: Benzene reacts rapidly by addition; cyclohexene reacts slowly by substitution
choices.why: It's the other way round: cyclohexene adds Br2 rapidly, while benzene reacts slowly by substitution.

choices.text: Benzene doesn't react; cyclohexene reacts rapidly by substitution
choices.why: Benzene does react, slowly, to give bromobenzene, and cyclohexene gives the addition product 1,2-dibromocyclohexane.

explanation: Benzene is much less reactive than typical alkenes. Cyclohexene reacts rapidly with Br2 to give the addition product 1,2-dibromocyclohexane, but benzene reacts slowly (with an iron catalyst) and gives the substitution product C6H5Br and HBr, not an addition product.

prompt: Cyclohexene has ΔH°_hydrog = −118 kJ/mol. If benzene were a “cyclohexatriene” whose three double bonds each behaved like cyclohexene's, how much heat would its hydrogenation release, in kJ/mol?
explanation: 3 × 118 = 354 kJ/mol. The section expects ΔH°_hydrog for “cyclohexatriene” to be a bit less than this, because conjugation adds a little stability. Benzene's actual value is only −206 kJ/mol.

prompt: What is the measured heat of hydrogenation of benzene?

choices.text: −206 kJ/mol
−354 kJ/mol
choices.why: That is three times cyclohexene's value, the amount expected for a “cyclohexatriene.” Benzene releases much less.

choices.text: −230 kJ/mol
choices.why: That is the value for 1,3-cyclohexadiene, a conjugated diene.

choices.text: −118 kJ/mol
choices.why: That is the value for cyclohexene, an isolated alkene.

explanation: Benzene's actual ΔH°_hydrog is −206 kJ/mol, compared with −118 kJ/mol for cyclohexene and −230 kJ/mol for 1,3-cyclohexadiene (Figure 15.2.1).

prompt: The expected heat of hydrogenation of “cyclohexatriene” is about −354 kJ/mol, but benzene's actual value is −206 kJ/mol. By how many kJ/mol is benzene more stable than expected?
explanation: 354 − 206 = 148 kJ/mol (35.4 kcal/mol). Because benzene releases 148 kJ/mol less energy on hydrogenation than expected, it must have 148 kJ/mol less energy to begin with: it is more stable than expected by that amount.

prompt: Which releases more heat when hydrogenated to cyclohexane: 1,3-cyclohexadiene or benzene?

choices.text: 1,3-Cyclohexadiene, 230 kJ/mol versus 206 kJ/mol for benzene
Benzene, because it has three double bonds to hydrogenate instead of two
choices.why: Benzene has an extra double bond yet releases less heat (206 versus 230 kJ/mol), a sign of its special stability.

choices.text: Both release the same amount, 354 kJ/mol
choices.why: 354 kJ/mol is only the value expected for a “cyclohexatriene”; the measured values differ.

choices.text: Benzene, 354 kJ/mol versus 230 kJ/mol for the diene
choices.why: Benzene's measured value is 206 kJ/mol; 354 kJ/mol is the expected value it falls short of.

explanation: From Figure 15.2.1, 1,3-cyclohexadiene has ΔH°_hydrog = −230 kJ/mol and benzene −206 kJ/mol. Even with three double bonds, benzene releases less heat than the diene, which shows how much more stable it is than a simple “cyclohexatriene.”

prompt: Why is ΔH°_hydrog of 1,3-cyclohexadiene (−230 kJ/mol) a bit less than twice that of cyclohexene (−118 kJ/mol)?

choices.text: Conjugated dienes are more stable than isolated dienes
Isolated dienes are more stable than conjugated dienes
choices.why: It's the reverse: the conjugated diene is more stable, so it releases a bit less heat.

choices.text: Only one of its two double bonds takes up hydrogen
choices.why: Both double bonds are hydrogenated to give cyclohexane; that's why the value is close to twice cyclohexene's.

choices.text: 1,3-Cyclohexadiene has the same special stability as benzene
choices.why: The diene falls short of twice cyclohexene's value by only a few kJ/mol; benzene falls short of its expected value by 148 kJ/mol.

explanation: As noted in Section 14.1, conjugated dienes are more stable than isolated dienes, so 1,3-cyclohexadiene releases a bit less than twice cyclohexene's heat of hydrogenation: 230 kJ/mol rather than 2 × 118 = 236 kJ/mol.

prompt: Twice cyclohexene's heat of hydrogenation is 2 × 118 = 236 kJ/mol. By how many kJ/mol does the heat released by 1,3-cyclohexadiene (230 kJ/mol) fall short of this?
explanation: 236 − 230 = 6 kJ/mol. That small shortfall reflects the extra stability of a conjugated diene. Compare benzene, whose heat of hydrogenation falls 148 kJ/mol short of the 354 kJ/mol expected.

prompt: Benzene releases 148 kJ/mol less heat on hydrogenation than expected for “cyclohexatriene.” What does this tell us?

choices.text: Benzene is 148 kJ/mol more stable than expected
Benzene is 148 kJ/mol less stable than expected
choices.why: Releasing less energy means benzene started lower in energy, so it is more stable, not less.

choices.text: Hydrogenation of benzene absorbs heat
choices.why: Benzene's ΔH°_hydrog is −206 kJ/mol, so the reaction still releases heat, just less than expected.

choices.text: Benzene has only two double bonds
choices.why: Benzene is still hydrogenated all the way to cyclohexane; the smaller heat release reflects extra stability, not a missing double bond.

explanation: Because benzene releases less energy than expected during hydrogenation, it must have less energy to begin with. In other words, benzene is more stable than expected by 148 kJ/mol (35.4 kcal/mol).

prompt: What are the carbon–carbon bond lengths in benzene?

choices.text: All six are 139 pm, between single- and double-bond lengths
They alternate: three are 154 pm and three are 134 pm
choices.why: All six bonds have the same length, 139 pm; benzene doesn't have alternating single and double bonds.

choices.text: All six are 134 pm, the length of a typical double bond
choices.why: Benzene's bonds, 139 pm, are longer than a typical double bond (134 pm).

choices.text: All six are 154 pm, the length of a typical single bond
choices.why: Benzene's bonds, 139 pm, are shorter than a typical single bond (154 pm).

explanation: All of benzene's carbon–carbon bonds are 139 pm long, intermediate between typical single (154 pm) and double (134 pm) bonds, and an electrostatic potential map shows the same electron density in all six.

prompt: What is the C–C–C bond angle in benzene, in degrees?
explanation: Benzene is a planar molecule with the shape of a regular hexagon. All C–C–C bond angles are 120°, all six carbons are sp2-hybridized, and each carbon has a p orbital perpendicular to the plane of the ring.

prompt: Which description of benzene's shape and bonding is correct?

choices.text: Planar regular hexagon; every carbon sp2, with a p orbital perpendicular to the ring
Puckered ring; every carbon sp3
choices.why: Benzene is planar, and its carbons are sp2-hybridized.

choices.text: Planar hexagon; carbons alternate between sp2 and sp3
choices.why: All six carbons are equivalent and sp2-hybridized.

choices.text: Planar regular hexagon; every carbon sp2, with a p orbital in the plane of the ring
choices.why: Each p orbital is perpendicular to the plane of the ring, which lets it overlap sideways with both neighbors.

explanation: Benzene is a planar molecule with the shape of a regular hexagon. All six carbon atoms are sp2-hybridized, and each has a p orbital perpendicular to the plane of the six-membered ring.

prompt: Why can't benzene be described by three localized π bonds?

choices.text: Each p orbital overlaps equally well with both of its neighbors
Its p orbitals lie in the plane of the ring and can't overlap
choices.why: The p orbitals are perpendicular to the ring plane, and they do overlap, with both neighbors.

choices.text: It has only three π electrons, too few for three π bonds
choices.why: Benzene has six π electrons, one in each carbon's p orbital.

choices.text: Its carbons are sp3-hybridized and have no p orbitals
choices.why: All six carbons are sp2-hybridized, and each has a p orbital.

explanation: Because all six carbons and all six p orbitals are equivalent, no p orbital can be said to overlap only one neighbor. Each overlaps equally well with both neighbors, so all six π electrons are free to move about the entire ring (Figure 15.2.2b).

prompt: Which statement about benzene's two resonance forms is correct?

choices.text: Neither is correct by itself; the true structure lies somewhere in between
Benzene switches rapidly back and forth between the two forms
choices.why: Resonance forms aren't real structures that interconvert; benzene is a single hybrid of the two.

choices.text: One form is the true structure and the other is a minor contributor
choices.why: The two forms are equivalent, and neither is correct by itself.

choices.text: The two forms differ in the positions of the carbon atoms
choices.why: Resonance forms differ only in where the electrons are drawn; the atoms stay in place.

explanation: In resonance terms, benzene is a hybrid of two equivalent forms. Neither form is correct by itself; the true structure is somewhere in between and can't be drawn with our usual conventions. This resonance makes benzene more stable and less reactive than a typical alkene.

prompt: Chemists sometimes draw benzene as a hexagon with a circle inside. What is the limitation of this drawing?

choices.text: It doesn't show how many π electrons are in the ring
It implies the double bonds are localized
choices.why: The circle does the opposite: it shows that all the carbon–carbon bonds are equivalent.

choices.text: It suggests the ring is not planar
choices.why: The circle says nothing against planarity; its problem is with counting electrons.

choices.text: It can't be used for rings that carry substituents
choices.why: The problem is that a circle doesn't indicate the number of π electrons, which is why the book uses line-bond structures.

explanation: A circle shows that the carbon–carbon bonds are equivalent, but it doesn't indicate the number of π electrons in the ring. That's why the book draws benzene and other aromatic compounds as single line-bond structures, which let us keep count of π electrons.

prompt: Benzene's six p atomic orbitals combine in a cyclic manner to give six π molecular orbitals. How many of these molecular orbitals are bonding?
explanation: The three low-energy molecular orbitals, ψ_1, ψ_2 and ψ_3, are bonding combinations, and the three high-energy orbitals are antibonding (Figure 15.2.3).

prompt: Benzene's π molecular orbitals ψ_2 and ψ_3 are described as degenerate. What does that mean?

choices.text: They have the same energy
They have nodes passing through two ring carbons
choices.why: That describes ψ_3 and ψ_4*. Degenerate means equal in energy.

choices.text: They are antibonding and empty
choices.why: ψ_2 and ψ_3 are bonding orbitals, and both are filled.

choices.text: They are the lowest-energy orbitals of the set
choices.why: ψ_1 is the single lowest-energy orbital; ψ_2 and ψ_3 lie above it, at equal energy.

explanation: Orbitals with the same energy are said to be degenerate. In benzene, the bonding orbitals ψ_2 and ψ_3 are degenerate, as are the antibonding orbitals ψ_4* and ψ_5*.

prompt: Nodes pass through ring carbon atoms in benzene's ψ_3 and ψ_4* orbitals. On how many carbons does each of these orbitals have no π electron density?
explanation: Figure 15.2.3 notes that ψ_3 and ψ_4* have no π electron density on two carbons, because a node passes through those atoms.

prompt: In the molecular orbital picture, where are benzene's six π electrons?

choices.text: Two in each of the three bonding orbitals, ψ_1, ψ_2 and ψ_3
One in each of the six π molecular orbitals
choices.why: Electrons pair up in the lowest orbitals; the three antibonding orbitals are empty.

choices.text: Two each in ψ_1, ψ_2 and the antibonding ψ_4*
choices.why: ψ_3 is a bonding orbital with the same energy as ψ_2, and it fills before any antibonding orbital.

choices.text: All six in the lowest orbital, ψ_1
choices.why: An orbital holds at most two electrons, so six electrons fill three orbitals.

explanation: The six p electrons of benzene occupy the three bonding molecular orbitals, two in each, and are delocalized over the entire conjugated system. The three antibonding orbitals are empty.

prompt: Pyridine is a flat, hexagonal molecule with 120° bond angles that undergoes substitution rather than addition, much like benzene. What best explains this?

choices.text: Like benzene, it has a ring of p orbitals holding an aromatic sextet of π electrons
Its nitrogen lone pair joins the π system to give eight π electrons
choices.why: Pyridine has a sextet of π electrons. Its nitrogen lone pair lies in the plane of the ring and isn't part of the π system (Section 15.5).

choices.text: Its ring atoms are sp3, so it has no double bonds to add to
choices.why: Its flat shape and 120° angles fit sp2 ring atoms, each with a p orbital, as in benzene.

choices.text: Its nitrogen breaks the ring's conjugation, so it reacts like an alkane
choices.why: Pyridine behaves like benzene, which depends on an unbroken ring of overlapping p orbitals.

explanation: Pyridine's π orbitals look like benzene's: each of the six ring atoms has a p orbital with one electron, giving an aromatic sextet (Exercise 15.2.1). That's why it is flat with 120° angles and prefers substitution to addition.
